title: Pathways to Information: Types of Knowledge
author: Harriett Janetos
summary: Harriett Janetos opens a series on comprehension by asking how an average teacher can make good in-the-moment decisions when class discussion cannot be scripted. Drawing on Carl Hendrick, she frames great teaching as navigating the tension between students' cognitive constraints and teachers' instructional freedom, with long feedback loops making errors hard to detect. She then turns to strategic knowledge, one of four types of knowledge in problem solving, arguing that strategy instruction can give both students and teachers a visible record of thinking to anchor contingent decisions. Linking this to varied retrieval practice and to Catherine Snow's definition of comprehension, she closes by listing questions about knowledge, language and strategy that the next installments will address.
points: Teaching cannot depend on saints and superstars, so research-based constraints and structures should help ordinary teachers make better decisions.
Long feedback loops in teaching mean mistakes can go unnoticed for months, unlike in chess or sport.
Contingent scaffolding means the next teacher move depends on what students say, which makes discussion hard to script.
Written student output such as a graphic organizer or summary paragraph gives the teacher signposts and anchors student thinking.
Varied retrieval of knowledge across modalities and contexts may reconcile the strategies versus knowledge-building divide.
quotes: He stopped me in the breezeway for a moment of lamentation, concluding that the teaching profession simply doesn’t accommodate your "average" teacher. If he was right, then we've got a big problem since most of us are average.

There’s a term for this strategic knowledge—contingent scaffolding—which simply means that your next teacher move is contingent upon a student move. It’s not four-dimensional chess; it’s just everyday teaching to three-dimensional children.

Successfully navigating the tension between the constraints on a student’s capacity to learn and the freedom a teacher has to design a myriad of lessons in a variety of ways is what Hendrick calls great teaching. Simply speaking, we need to put teachers in a position where they are equipped to make decisions that lead to better outcomes for their students.

Specifically, for the student, it anchors thought by pinning it to paper or a white board. For the teacher, it can provide a structure that might be missing from the transient nature of a whole-class discussion where the teacher is orchestrating all the moves.

The question is: What can help structure a teacher’s train of thought when there’s no one around to press recording in progress? That's what well-developed strategy instruction can provide—a record of student thought made visible for reference and redirection—and timely reminders to the teacher to move on or go back and reteach if it’s evident that there was a breakdown in comprehension.

Comprehension relies on knowledge, which is expressed through language—through the vocabulary and sentence structures nestled within paragraphs. Therefore, unlocking the vocabulary, syntax, and paragraph structure (and the relationships between all of these literacy components) of what is read—releases that knowledge (extracting) to be used in contexts beyond any particular piece read (constructing).
